newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Views mixed on Irish Feb credit growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Views mixed on Irish Feb credit growth.

text.p: Opinion is divided on the pace of Irish credit growth in February with some analysts forecasting a slowdown in lending while others look for a moderate acceleration and yet others expect credit to remain unchanged.

But analysts say that unless the figure is well out of line, its market impact should be reasonably muted as the Irish pound's exchange rate and the approach of economic and monetary union (EMU) are more relevant to interest rate policy at present.

Riada Stockbrokers expect the adjusted annual rate of growth in private sector credit to rise to 15.4 percent from 15.2 percent in January when the central bank releases the data at 1630 local time (1530 GMT) on Thursday.

"The season appears to have started quite early in terms of the housing market. It's probably been quite a busy month for mortgages in February so we are pencilling in a modest acceleration in mortgage lending growth to 14.1 percent from 14.0 percent in January," Riada economist Padraic Garvey said.

But Oliver Mangan, bond economist at AIB Group Treasury, expects credit growth to remain unchanged from January's level at 15.2 percent while NCB Stockbrokers forecast a deceleration in underlying credit growth to 14.5 percent.

"Given the acceleration last year, you'd have to have an extra bit going for you this year to push it higher. It's the level of outstanding credit so your base is rising all the time," Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers said.
Whatever the number, it is unlikely to have major monetary policy implications at present, analysts say.

"The inflation scenario is quite good and while that remains the case, even if credit is growing quite strongly, it shouldn't have any direct repercussions on interest rate policy," said Riada's Garvey.
"Interest rate policy is going to remain steady for the foreseeable future and it would be very unlikely if tomorrow's number is going to change that."
First quarter Exchequer Borrowing figures, also due for release at 1630 local time (1530 GMT) on Thursday, are expected to show that Ireland's public finances remain in good order.
Analysts expect the end-March Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) to come in somewhere between 150 and 300 million Irish pounds, well below 561 million at end-March last year.
Revenue buoyancy, delayed value-added tax (VAT) receipts, subdued spending and an increase in EU receipts are among the factors seen depressing borrowing.
"Tax receipts were very strong in the first quarter...while EU receipts in the first three months of 1997 were 170 million Irish pounds higher than in the same period last year," AIB's Mangan said.
"We see a combination of these two factors working to produce what we think should be a very low EBR figure."

Analysts said a good figure would confirm that the government was well on course to meet or even undershoot its 1997 EBR target of 637 million Irish pounds but was unlikely to have much impact on the bond market where the positive public finance story was already well known.
"I don't think it'll be a factor that will push the Irish market ahead but it will underpin it," said Mangan.
